project.name: python-regos-integrations
project.description: FastAPI gateway service that exposes a unified REST interface over the REGOS API and hosts pluggable client integrations (Telegram bots, SMS gateways, EDO/e-invoicing providers, CRM channels, marketplaces, and a TSD warehouse PWA). Wrapper services validate REGOS calls with Pydantic models, while clients connect via webhooks and external handlers backed by Redis and MariaDB. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the project README to understand what this service is: a FastAPI gateway that connects REGOS to external providers such as Telegram bots, SMS gateways, EDO, CRM channels, and marketplaces. The README also documents the two extension mechanisms that drive everything: REGOS API service wrappers and pluggable integration clients. Read it as the roadmap for the rest of this tour, since every later step elaborates on a concept introduced here.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: server.py is the runtime entry point: its create_app factory builds the FastAPI app, registers exception handlers, and wires startup/shutdown hooks that restore and tear down active integrations. This file is the root of the dependency graph, so understanding what it imports gives you a bird's-eye view of how routing, clients, and core infrastructure are stitched together. Everything else in the tour is something server.py reaches, directly or transitively.
tour.languageLesson: FastAPI apps are commonly assembled with an application factory (create_app) plus lifespan startup/shutdown handlers. This lets the gateway restore previously connected integrations on boot and shut them down cleanly, instead of relying on import-time side effects.

tour.title: Routing & Client Dispatch
tour.description: The routers are the bridge between incoming HTTP traffic and the integration clients. routes/clients.py holds the key-to-client mapping that exposes every provider under /clients/<key>/... and dispatches integration, UI, and external webhook requests to the right handler, while healthcheck.py provides a simple liveness probe. This is where a newly added client becomes reachable from the outside world, so it is the natural second stop after the entry point.

tour.title: The RegosAPI Facade
tour.description: core/api/regos_api.py is the single facade every integration uses to talk to REGOS, exposed through the `async with RegosAPI(id) as api` pattern with retry handling and batch support. Underneath, core/api/client.py is the async HTTP client that adds OAuth bearer auth, token-bucket rate limiting, 429 cooldown/retry, and gzip handling. Together they centralize all REGOS communication so individual clients never deal with raw HTTP — this facade has one of the highest fan-in counts in the codebase.
tour.languageLesson: Python async context managers (`async with`) let RegosAPI acquire and release resources — auth tokens, HTTP sessions, rate-limiter state — around a block of awaited calls, guaranteeing cleanup even when a request fails.

tour.title: A Concrete API Service
tour.description: Building on the facade from Step 4, core/api/docs/cheque.py is a representative `*Service` wrapper: it exposes REGOS cheque-document endpoints (get list, get by uuids) as typed async methods reached via `api.docs.cheque`. The companion conventions doc explains the project structure, naming, logging, and method-signature rules every service class must follow. Study this pair to learn exactly how to add a new REGOS API service, mirroring the README's first extension recipe.

tour.title: Schema & Contract Layer
tour.description: Every request and response is validated by Pydantic v2 schemas. schemas/api/base.py defines the shared response envelopes (base, error, array, add-result) reused everywhere — it is the single most depended-upon file in the project — and schemas/api/docs/cheque.py shows a concrete entity contract with sort enums, the model, and a date-validated request that pairs with the Step 5 service. The schema conventions doc captures the entity-file template these all follow.
tour.languageLesson: Pydantic v2 generic models let one base envelope (e.g. an array or add-result response) be parameterized by the concrete entity type, giving every endpoint a consistent, type-checked response shape with no boilerplate per resource.

tour.title: Integration Client Base Interfaces
tour.description: The second extension mechanism is the pluggable client. clients/base.py is the abstract base defining the lifecycle every provider implements (connect/disconnect/handle_webhook/handle_external), and the schemas/integration base contracts specialize it — integration_base for generic requests, sms and telegram bases adding provider-specific capabilities like send_messages. These interfaces are what a new client extends before being registered in the routing map from Step 3.
tour.languageLesson: Python ABCs (abstract base classes) declare a contract of required methods; subclasses that omit one cannot be instantiated. This is how the gateway guarantees every client implements the full connect/disconnect/handle_webhook/handle_external lifecycle.

tour.title: Simple Client Examples
tour.description: Now see the base interfaces realized. clients/eskiz_sms/main.py is a minimal SMS client: it manages the provider auth token and sends messages, implementing the SMS base from Step 7. clients/telegram_bot_orders/main.py is a richer Telegram bot with Redis-backed stream workers, webhook/long-polling handling, and cart management. Compare them to see how much (or how little) a client needs depending on the provider's complexity, both talking to REGOS through the Step 4 facade.

tour.title: A CRM-Channel Client with State
tour.description: clients/meta_leadgen_crm_channel/main.py is one of the most complete integrations: it handles Meta OAuth authorization, webhook ingestion, a Redis stream worker, and UI/external/lead flows that sync leads into REGOS CRM. Its persistence layer is the mlg_page_map SQL table, which durably maps a Meta page_id to its connected REGOS integration so webhooks can be routed back to the right tenant. This step shows how a stateful channel ties together routing, the RegosAPI facade, Redis, and its own database table.
tour.languageLesson: SQL migrations should be ordered and idempotent. The mlg_page_map InnoDB table uses page_id as a stable lookup key so incoming Meta webhooks can resolve which REGOS integration to dispatch to, decoupling provider identifiers from internal integration IDs.

tour.title: Core Infrastructure
tour.description: The clients you just saw lean on a shared infrastructure layer. core/redis.py provides JSON caching, locks, TTL, and streams (the backbone of the bot workers); core/mariadb.py is the async DB access layer behind tables like mlg_page_map; core/scheduler.py registers recurring integration tasks with REGOS; and core/logger.py plus config/settings.py supply centralized logging and environment-driven configuration. These cross-cutting services are high fan-in dependencies used across every client and API service.

tour.title: The TSD PWA Frontend
tour.description: One integration ships its own user interface: the TSD warehouse data-collection client. clients/tsd/main.py exposes warehouse actions over REGOS on the backend, while the React PWA mounts in main.jsx, wires routes and context providers in App.jsx, and talks to the gateway through the lib/api.js fetch wrapper. This shows how a client can pair server-side REGOS logic with a self-contained browser app served from the same gateway.
tour.languageLesson: React Context providers (here App, I18n, and Toast) supply shared state down the component tree without prop drilling, while a thin fetch wrapper centralizes API base-path resolution so every page issues requests the same way.

tour.title: Containerization & Deployment
tour.description: The Dockerfile defines how the whole gateway is packaged. It is a multi-stage build: a Node 20 stage compiles the TSD PWA assets from Step 11, then a Python 3.12-slim stage installs dependencies and copies in the compiled frontend plus the application code from Steps 2-10. The result is a single image that serves both the FastAPI backend and the PWA, keeping the runtime image lean by leaving build tooling behind in the earlier stage.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker builds use multiple FROM statements so heavy build tooling (Node, compilers) lives only in early stages. Copying just the compiled artifacts into the final Python stage keeps the production image small and free of build-time dependencies.

tour.title: Contributor & Agent Guide
tour.description: Finish with AGENTS.md, the contributor guide that ties the tour together: it documents the authoritative sources, REGOS API and webhook conventions, integration code style, and a code-review checklist. Having walked the entry point, facade, schemas, clients, infrastructure, frontend, and deployment, you now have the context to read these conventions and confidently add a new API service or a new integration client following the project's established patterns.
